name: Pont du Gard
hint: Roman engineers stood arches on piers. Pier tops below the deck make strong springing points - fill each opening with an arch and prop the road from it.

history.name: Pont du Gard
history.span: Largest arch ≈ 24.5 m · 48.8 m high · top tier 275 m
facts: Its stones were cut so precisely that most of it stands without mortar or clamps - friction and gravity hold it together.
The aqueduct it carried ran about 50 km to Nîmes at an average gradient of only 1 in 3,000, delivering an estimated 40,000 m³ of water a day.
In 1743–47 the engineer Henri Pitot built a road bridge alongside the lower tier - the road you are building here.
history.why: The highest of all Roman aqueduct bridges, and proof that a round arch turns heavy loads into pure compression that stone can carry for two thousand years.
history.note: Historically masonry. Masonry arrives with the Iron Road campaign - until then, build the arches in wood and steel.
